Text | Er Mu

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Translating between Chinese and English is a strange business. How would you put “voice” into Chinese? As shēngyīn, “sound”? But English already has “sound” for that. As kǒuyīn, “accent”? English seems to have “accent” for that too. So what does “voice” actually mean? It describes “the physical sound that comes out of our mouths when we speak.” How does that strike you as a translation?

Odds and ends

Rain spattering against the window, wind gusting outside, I was wondering what to write about this time when a question popped into my odd little brain: does the sound of our voice ever change?

The first thing that comes to mind, of course, is the voice breaking at puberty, something everyone goes through. Boys especially: one day between the ages of 12 and 16 they notice their throat feels a little different, and their voice sounds like someone else’s. Before puberty, a child’s larynx sits fairly high in the neck. As puberty progresses, it moves lower and lower, and the vocal folds grow larger and thicker. The voice goes from childish and piping to deep and more “manly.” How much deeper varies from person to person. A boy’s voice typically drops by about an octave, and a gifted few become walking subwoofers. Girls’ voices drop at puberty too, though much less noticeably than boys’: usually by only about three whole tones. The whole process typically takes about a year, and by around 17 our voices have settled and rarely change much afterward.

The vocal apparatus

That holds until old age, when the body goes into decline. The larynx stiffens and its cartilage usually calcifies; the vocal folds lose much of their elasticity and flexibility, and the muscles in them waste away, leaving them thinner and weaker. Our ribs calcify too, and our lungs shrink and stiffen. These changes, in the organs of speech and in the respiratory system that powers them, give us an “old person’s voice.”

So the voice changes in childhood because of hormones and in old age because our organs wear out. But in adulthood, when hormones and organs are both stable, can our voice, or our accent, change all of a sudden? (I don’t mean an accent we pick up deliberately by imitation.)

When we speak, our voice carries more than the meaning of our words. It also says a great deal about us: what kind of person we are, how we feel at that moment, where we come from, and so on. A Chinese saying has it that when people from the same hometown meet far from home, their eyes fill with tears, and accent really is the quickest way to spot someone from back home. Perhaps you’ve had this experience too: you meet a friend from your hometown whose Mandarin is so polished that most people can’t tell where they’re from, yet in a sound or two you always catch something familiar. The accent of home is that powerful.

Can you imagine someone from Sichuan, whose speech is peppered with the local expletive chuizi, suddenly calling out “Fresh Xinjiang lamb skewers!” in the singsong of a Xinjiang street vendor?

During the Second World War, Germany occupied Norway. In an Allied air raid on Oslo, a woman named Astrid was hit by shrapnel and tumbled down a steep bank by the road. Astrid was Norwegian born and bred, but the incident left her with a serious brain injury. Stranger still, her accent no longer sounded Norwegian. She sounded like a foreigner. The neurologist who helped with her recovery wrote in his notes: “She complains that when she goes shopping she is constantly taken for a German, and the shop assistants refuse to sell her anything.” In fact, she had never set foot outside Norway, and the change in her accent was truly baffling. The shopkeepers put it down to her being a German collaborator, which is why they refused to serve her. The sudden change left Astrid shaken and at a loss, and she began to doubt herself.

What changed Astrid’s accent was a rare condition called foreign accent syndrome. It is usually caused by damage to the brain from a head injury, a stroke or something similar. Patients’ accents change, and the people around them decide, based on their own experience, which region or country the new accent belongs to. The shopkeepers and assistants took Astrid’s new accent for German, but had she been placed next to an actual German, people would have found that she sounded nothing like one. Perhaps she was heard as German because the shopkeepers loathed the Germans who had invaded Norway, so any accent unlike their own went into the “German” box. In other words, had France occupied Norway at the time, Astrid’s new accent might well have been heard as French.

Damage to the parts of the cerebral cortex that control the organs of speech makes the patient’s voice sound strange. They have not lost the ability to speak, but their pronunciation and speech rhythm turn odd and unfamiliar to those around them, who then fall back on stereotypes and mistake it for a regional or foreign accent.

Astrid’s story astonished me. So in real life, someone’s accent really can change overnight. It also made me marvel at how remarkable the human brain is. World peace and good health: may everyone stay safe and well!

This seems to be the first time one of our posts has landed on a holiday. I’m sure you know what day it is: Qixi, the Chinese Valentine’s Day. Here’s wishing all lovers a happy ending, and to those already together, happiness that lasts forever!

Reference: Trevor Cox, Now You’re Talking
